title: How did the United States win the race to the Moon?
subject: histoire
description: Sputnik, Laika, Gagarin: in the late 1950s, everything suggested the USSR would reach the Moon first. Twelve years after Sputnik, it was two Americans who set foot on it.
author: myra-houser

hero.hook: For years, the Soviets led the race. On July 20, 1969, it was two Americans who walked on the Moon.

blocks.text: Of all the episodes of the [[Cold War]], the race to the Moon is one of the most closely followed by the public. For decades, American and Soviet scientists and engineers developed the technologies needed to circle the Earth and then leave it behind. Some aspects of the rivalry were frightening, like proxy wars or the nuclear threat.

Others made people smile, like the [[Kitchen Debate]], a verbal sparring match between American vice president Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in **1959**. The Space Race, for its part, captivated the whole world and stirred national pride. In the 1950s, everything suggested that the USSR would reach the Moon first.

sections.title: Sputnik, Laika and the first living beings in space

blocks.text: The Soviet Union put the first satellites into orbit, the [[Sputnik]] series, starting in **1957**. In **1961**, [[Yuri Gagarin]] became the first human to fly in space. The United States, for its part, had been sending several generations of monkeys, all named Albert, beyond the atmosphere since the 1940s.

In **1957**, Laika, a stray dog, became the first living creature to orbit the Earth, aboard Sputnik 2. The authorities said she had lived for a week in orbit. Later research showed that she overheated and died in panic soon after the flight began.

In **1961**, the United States sent a chimpanzee named Ham into space, then, later that year, another named Enos, who completed a full orbit of the Earth. Both came back alive. Ham even enjoyed a long life after his journey.

sections.title: Gemini, then Apollo: the goal set by Kennedy

blocks.text: In the 1960s, both countries set themselves the same goal: to put a man on the Moon before the other. In **1962**, John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. He dreamed of going all the way to the Moon, but NASA, the American space agency, worried about his health over repeated missions and grounded him. Glenn left the agency and went into politics.

The [[Gemini program]] sent a total of **16 astronauts** into flight to perfect piloting and docking between spacecraft. It ran until **1966**, when the Apollo missions took over. President John F. Kennedy had commissioned them in **1961**, alongside Gemini, with a clear goal: to land a man on the Moon and bring him safely back to Earth.

sections.title: July 20, 1969: one small step for man

blocks.text: Buzz Aldrin, Neil Armstrong and Michael Collins had all flown in the Gemini program when they were chosen for Apollo. Their names remain attached to the American victory. The trio lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on **July 16, 1969**, aboard Apollo 11.

blocks.caption: The lunar module climbs back toward Collins's spacecraft, with the Earth on the horizon.

blocks.text: On **July 20**, Collins stayed in orbit around the Moon while Aldrin and Armstrong went down in the lunar module. They landed on the [[Sea of Tranquility]], a vast dark plain. Six hours later, Armstrong stepped out of the module: he was the first human to walk on the Moon. Aldrin followed. "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind": Armstrong's words effectively closed the race.
From the surface of the Moon, Armstrong and Aldrin spoke by telephone with the White House, while television stations around the world broadcast the event live.

sections.title: From race to cooperation in space

blocks.text: Americans and Soviets still competed on technology until the end of the Cold War, but the Moon walk marked the end of the Space Race. The two countries moved toward cooperation. In **1975**, they launched [[Apollo-Soyuz]], the first joint space program: an American spacecraft and a Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit.

blocks.caption: The handshake between Thomas Stafford and Alexei Leonov in the Apollo-Soyuz docking module, July 1975.

blocks.text: That first paved the way for today's exploration, largely carried out jointly, as aboard the International Space Station. In all, **12 Americans** have walked on the Moon, the last in **1972**. Since then, the Soviet Union, China, India and Japan have all landed uncrewed craft on its surface. The race ended in 1969, but it fed cooperation and a lasting human fascination with space.

events.detail: The USSR puts the first satellite into orbit, then the dog Laika aboard Sputnik 2.

events.title: Gagarin and Kennedy's goal
events.detail: First man in space; Kennedy sets the course: a man on the Moon, brought back safely.

events.title: John Glenn in orbit
events.detail: The first American to circle the Earth.

events.title: Apollo 11
events.detail: Armstrong, then Aldrin, walk on the Sea of Tranquility.

events.title: Apollo-Soyuz
events.detail: The first joint space program between the two rivals.

blocks.text: Outpaced by Sputnik and Gagarin, the United States won the race to the Moon thanks to the goal Kennedy set in 1961, the Gemini and then Apollo flights, and the Apollo 11 mission of July 20, 1969, before rivalry gave way to cooperation.
